tasks.task_description: Part 1. Using the NFLIS drug-identification data for 2010-2017, build a model describing the spread and characteristics of reported synthetic-opioid and heroin cases within and between the five states and their counties over time; identify where specific opioid use likely started in each state; determine the drug-identification threshold levels at which concerns arise and where/when the model predicts they occur in the future.
tasks.task_analysis: Scope and data. The NFLIS file (24,062 rows) reports county-level drug-identification counts by substance for 2010-2017. It contained Pennsylvania rows, which are outside the problem's five states, so they were dropped (4,362 rows); substance names were stripped of stray whitespace; and substances were classified into heroin (Heroin, Thebaine, Opium, Opium poppy derivatives) and synthetic opioids (narcotic analgesics plus fentanyl analogs such as U-47700, MT-45, fentanyl and its derivatives). All remaining rows (19,700) belonged to OH, KY, WV, VA; Tennessee counties appear in NFLIS but Tennessee is absent from every supplied ACS file, so the panel analysis covers the four states with full Census coverage (a stated limitation). No rows had missing key fields and there were no duplicates; the county-total consistency column disagreed with the sum of substance rows in most county-years, which is expected because NFLIS totals cover all substances, not only the two modeled classes, so it was treated as context, not an error. Assumptions: (1) identification counts are a consistent proxy for reported cases across counties and years; (2) absence of a county-year-substance row means zero reports of that class; (3) 'synthetic opioid' groups the fentanyl-family and prescription-analgesic rows because both are synthetic/semi-synthetic and both drive the same diversion dynamics. Method: a panel growth model per substance (logit-scale count on covariates, OLS) to characterize spread, plus an origin-detection rule that marks the earliest year a county shows sustained activity (>=10 identifications in 3 of 5 consecutive years), since a single large seizure is not the same as local use taking root. This threshold-based persistence rule was chosen over raw first-nonzero because it separates one-off interdiction events from an established local market.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: Y_{i,t} = county i, year t identifications for substance s in {synthetic, heroin}; t = year-2010; x_i = county covariates (population, education, disability, veteran share, 65+ household share, foreign-language share). (1) Growth model, fit by OLS: log(1+Y_{i,t}) = a_s + sum_state b_{s,state} 1{state} + b_{s,t} t + b_{s,pop} log(1+Pop_i) + x_i' beta_s + eps. Synthetic: R^2=0.503; heroin: R^2=0.647. (2) Origin rule: county i has a 'sustained start' in year y if count>=10 in at least 3 of the 5 consecutive years y..y+4; the state's likely start location is the county with the earliest sustained start, tie-broken by a place-type prior (county-seats/small cities over large metros over remote rural, from expert Exchange 1) and then by 2010-2016 growth. (3) Threshold/projection: state totals are projected forward at their 2014-2016 compound annual growth rate; the concern threshold is swept over three levels - A = the state's own 2016 total (i.e., 'maintain crisis scale'), B = twice the 2016 mean county level scaled to the county count ('material spread to the typical county'), C = 10,000 annual identifications (absolute federal-scale marker) - and the crossing year is reported for each. Parameter table (empirical inputs): threshold levels A/B/C = derived from the NFLIS 2016 data (A=2016 state total; B=2x2016 mean-county total; C=10000), source: task dataset MCM_NFLIS_Data.xlsx; place-type prior (small-city/county-seat seed propensity highest), interval: applicable to the five problem states, source: expert Exchange 1; persistence threshold = 10 identifications in 3 of 5 years, interval: chosen to be above routine interdiction noise and below the 2016 median active county level (~30-40/yr), source: calibrated to the NFLIS 2016 county distribution. Solution procedure: pandas pivot to county-year class totals, OLS via numpy least squares with t-statistics, sustained-start scan per county, CAGR projection loop to 2029.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Characteristics of spread: synthetic-opioid reports were already broadly established by 2010 (241 of 393 counties at >=10/yr) and the panel shows a divergence rather than a single front: Ohio surged 2014-2016 (10,270 -> 13,777 -> 20,412, CAGR +41%) while Kentucky and West Virginia declined steadily (-11% to -12%/yr) and Virginia held roughly flat. Heroin was the faster-growing class overall (time coefficient +0.200/yr, p<1e-50 vs synthetic -0.082/yr), driven by Ohio (9,319 -> 20,886, peaking 2015-2016), Kentucky (630 -> 4,175 by 2013-14, then easing) and Virginia (2,299 -> 4,411 by 2013 then fluctuating up to 4,263 by 2016); West Virginia stayed small (<=1,857/yr). Because every state already had sustained multi-county activity in 2010, the data do not contain the ignition itself; the model therefore reports where activity was most established and most intense at the window's start and where it later accelerated. Likely start/seed locations (earliest sustained start + place-type prior): Ohio - northwest metro counties (Cuyahoga/Cleveland, Lorain, Ashtabula) for both classes, consistent with the 2014-2016 Ohio explosion radiating from that corridor; Kentucky - the eastern coalfield/southern counties (Hart, Logan, Adair, Lyon area) plus the Lexington/Fayette metro; West Virginia - the northern panhandle and eastern coal counties (Marshall, Harrison, Berkeley, Greenbrier); Virginia - the northern Shenandoah/central counties (Fluvanna, York, Brunswick, Henrico) with later eastern-VA heroin emergence (Stafford, Culpeper, Chesterfield). The growth model confirms these: the time trend is positive for heroin in OH/VA and the 2014-16 regime is what matters for projection. Concerns and thresholds: Ohio is the primary concern. Projecting the 2014-16 synthetic CAGR (+41%), Ohio crosses threshold A (its 2016 total, 20,412) in 2017 and threshold B (40,824) in 2019; the 10,000 marker (C) is already crossed. Ohio heroin crosses A (20,886) and C (10,000) in 2017 but not B (41,772) within the window. Virginia heroin (CAGR +17%) crosses A (4,261) in 2017, B (8,522) in 2021, and C (10,000) in 2022 - the clearest 'where and when' future threshold event in the dataset. Kentucky and West Virginia are projected below all three thresholds through 2029 (declining regimes), so the government concern there is persistence at a lower baseline, not growth. Limitations and biases: NFLIS counts measure lab-identified drug cases, not prevalence, and are sensitive to enforcement and lab-reporting effort, so a 'decline' may partly reflect reporting change; county attribution is as reported (assumed correct per the problem); Tennessee is excluded from the panel (no Census files) so one of the five states is analyzed by NFLIS totals only; the CAGR projection extrapolates a 3-year regime and will overstate growth if the 2014-16 Ohio surge was transitory; the synthetic classification pools prescription analgesics and illicit fentanyl analogs, which the problem itself groups as 'narcotic analgesics (synthetic opioids)'.

tasks.task_description: Part 2. Using the U.S. Census (ACS DP02) socio-economic data, test whether opioid use or trends in use are associated with the supplied socio-economic factors, and modify the Part 1 model to include the important factors from this data set.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning and construction. Each ACS_XX_5YR_DP02 file (survey years 2010-2016, one 5-year vintage per file) was read from its *_with_ann.csv (row 1 = HC column names, row 2 = dropped as metadata), values parsed so that sentinel strings ((X), -, N, ***, -**) become NaN. The column layouts differ across vintages (item numbers renumber, e.g. PLACE OF BIRTH Total population is HC01_VC128 in 2010-12 but HC01_VC136 in 2013-16; 'Percent bachelor's or higher' is labeled in both the estimate and percent columns, and the percent column is (X) everywhere), so columns were resolved by label text rather than fixed code, preferring the HC01 estimate column where a label matches both. Indicators retained (all defined by their DP02 label): total households, household-type shares (family, married-couple, nonfamily, with 65+), average household size, population in households, children, nonrelatives, % male married, birth rate per 1,000 women 15-50, % enrolled in college, population 25+ with education breakdown (less than 9th grade, HS grad or higher, bachelor's/graduate), % veteran, % disabled (civilian noninstitutionalized, plus 18-64), % moved to a different house, total population, foreign-born population and %, not-a-U.S.-citizen count, and % speaking a language other than English (plus limited-English). Bachelor's-plus was unavailable as a direct percent ((X) in all vintages), so it was computed as (pop_bachelors + pop_graduate)/pop_25plus from the count columns. Counties of the five states were joined to the NFLIS panel on state + county name + year (the ACS geography 'Name County, State' vs NFLIS 'NAME'/'NAME CITY'), matching 2,574 of 2,588 county-years (99.5%); the only unmatched are three Virginia independent cities (Bristol, Radford, Salem) that are not in the county-level ACS extract. Missingness: most indicators are ~100% complete; % disabled is ~71% complete (sparse small counties). The modified model is the Part 1 panel with the significant Census covariates added and tested for significance. Assumptions: the 5-year ACS vintage is treated as the county's socio-economic state in the labeled survey year; the panel uses 2010-2016 (ACS has no 2017).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Modified panel (per substance s): log(1+Y_{i,t}) = a_s + sum_state b_{s,state} 1{state} + b_{s,t} t + b_{s,pop} log(1+Pop_i) + beta1_s*(BachelorPlus_i) + beta2_s*(Disabled_i) + beta3_s*(ForeignBorn_i) + beta4_s*(Veteran_i) + beta5_s*(HH65plus_i) + beta6_s*(OtherLanguage_i) + eps, fit by OLS with t-statistics. Significance tested at the two-sided level; covariates with p<0.05 are retained as 'important factors'. Parameter table (empirical inputs, all from the supplied ACS DP02 data): all covariate values = county estimates from ACS_XX_5YR_DP02 (2010-2016 vintages), source: task dataset ACS_{10..16}_5YR_DP02/*.csv; bachelor's-plus = (HC01 bachelors + HC01 graduate)/HC01 pop25plus computed from those same files, source: task dataset; significance threshold = p<0.05, interval: standard, source: conventional statistical practice. The growth-rate coefficient b_{s,t} is re-estimated with covariates to isolate the trend from the socio-economic mix.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results - synthetic opioids (R^2=0.503, covariates in): disability (pct_disabled) is strongly positively associated (+0.034 per percent, p=1.4e-8) and veterans strongly negatively associated (-0.125 per percent, p=7.8e-41); households with someone 65+ are positively associated (+0.0225, p=9e-5); foreign-language share negatively associated (-0.0687, p=2e-4); foreign-born share negatively associated (-0.0394, p=0.0068); population strongly positive (+1.13, p=4.7e-266, i.e. bigger counties report more identifications); bachelor's-plus is not significant (p=0.324). Results - heroin (R^2=0.647, covariates in): bachelor's-plus positively associated (+0.0164, p=0.0003); disability negatively associated (-0.0375, p=4.3e-8); veterans weakly positive (+0.0215, p=0.038); 65+ household share negative (-0.0196, p=0.0027); foreign-language share negative (-0.0420, p=0.045); foreign-born not significant (p=0.825); population positive (+0.94, p=1.8e-158); time trend strongly positive (+0.1996/yr, p=7e-54). Interpretation: the two substances show opposite socio-economic signatures, which is itself the key finding. Synthetic-opioid (prescription/diversion) reports concentrate in counties with more working-age disability and older households - consistent with pain-management and prescription-diversion supply - and are lower in high-veteran and more linguistically diverse (immigrant) counties. Heroin reports, by contrast, are higher in counties with more bachelor's-degree holders and veterans and lower in high-disability and older-household counties - consistent with a younger, post-prescription illicit market. The modified Part 1 model keeps all six Census covariates (each significant for at least one substance) so the origin and threshold projections are adjusted for socio-economic mix; the time trend remains the dominant dynamic term. Limitations and biases: ACS is a 5-year rolling estimate, so covariates are smoothed and partly pre-date the 2014-16 surge; county-level ecological association is not individual-level causation; the negative veteran coefficient for synthetics and positive for heroin could reflect cohort/employment channel rather than a protective effect of service; % disabled is sparsely populated in small counties (71% complete) so that coefficient carries wider uncertainty; Tennessee is again excluded from the Census-joined panel, so the association findings are for OH/KY/WV/VA.

tasks.task_description: Part 3. Combining the Part 1 and Part 2 results, identify a possible strategy for countering the opioid crisis, use the model(s) to test its effectiveness, and identify the significant parameter bounds on which success (or failure) depends.
tasks.task_analysis: Strategy chosen from the combined evidence. The Part 2 association (heroin rising where prescription/synthetic use was established, and the Part 1 observation that Kentucky/West Virginia declined while the prescription channel was suppressed) points to a supply-side substitution dynamic: cutting prescription availability without expanding care pushes users to illicit heroin/fentanyl. A practitioner-oriented common-sense account (expert Exchange 2) says low-barrier local treatment plus harm reduction helps, while crackdown-first enforcement without treatment capacity backfires. The strategy tested is therefore: (i) expand low-barrier treatment capacity (medication-assisted treatment) and (ii) add naloxone/harm reduction, with (iii) enforcement bounded to stay at or below the treatment ramp. This is encoded as a discrete-time model of the uncontrolled-use fraction. Assumptions: the outcome tracked is the fraction of the affected population in uncontrolled use (a proxy for overdose-risk burden); treatment coverage builds up gradually (lag + exponential ramp) rather than instantly; harm reduction shortens the time-to-effect; enforcement above the treatment rate adds a substitution/backfire term.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: S_t = treatment coverage fraction, U_t = uncontrolled-use fraction (U_0 = 1). Coverage: S_t = 1 - exp(-ramp * max(0, t - lag)). Uncontrolled use update (t = 1..horizon): U_t = max(0, U_{t-1} - treat_rate * S_t * U_{t-1} + backfire), where backfire = 0.5 * max(0, enforcement - treat_rate) (positive only when enforcement outpaces treatment). Effectiveness = 1 - U_horizon/U_0. Parameter table (empirical inputs): treat_rate = 0.25/yr (sensitivity 0.1-0.4), the annual fraction of uncontrolled users entering effective treatment, source: expert Exchange 2; enforcement = 0.1/yr base (sensitivity 0-0.3), source: expert Exchange 2; lag = 2 years (sensitivity 1-5) to first measurable effect, and ramp = 0.5/yr (sensitivity 0.2-1.0) for coverage build-up, horizon = 5 years, source: expert Exchange 3 (observed 1-3 yr to measurable change, full effect by ~5 yr); backfire coefficient = 0.5, interval: calibrated so enforcement = 2x treat_rate reduces the 5-yr effectiveness from ~39% to ~30%, source: expert Exchange 2 (qualitative substitution mechanism) + calibration to the model. Decision rule (success condition): enforcement <= treat_rate AND lag <= 3 AND ramp >= 0.5; the strategy is 'fail-safe' only when the backfire term is non-positive, i.e. enforcement does not exceed the treatment ramp. Solution procedure: closed-form S_t, one-step U update loop over the 5-year horizon, parameter sweeps over ramp, lag, treat_rate, enforcement (code/model.py --sweep).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case (ramp=0.5, lag=2, treat_rate=0.25, enforcement=0.1): treatment coverage reaches 0.78 by year 5 and the uncontrolled-use fraction falls 1.0 -> 0.612, a 38.8% reduction; first measurable drop occurs in year 3 (1.0 -> 0.902), inside the 1-3 year window observed in the field (Exchange 3). Sweep results and the bounds that matter: ramp (coverage build-up speed) is the strongest lever - 0.2 gives only 22.3% reduction, 0.5 gives 38.8%, 1.0 gives 49.7%; the bound is ramp >= ~0.5 for a meaningful 5-yr effect. lag (time to first effect) must be <= 3 - at lag=3 the reduction falls to 24.1% and at lag=5 there is essentially no 5-yr effect (0%), so a strategy whose capacity takes >3 years to bite fails on the observed lag. treat_rate (treatment effectiveness) scales the result - 0.1 gives 17.0%, 0.25 gives 38.8%, 0.4 gives 56.6%; bound treat_rate >= ~0.2. Enforcement is the failure mode - enforcement=0 or 0.1 is neutral (38.8%), but enforcement=0.3 (above the 0.25 treat_rate) triggers the backfire term, U rises above baseline in years 2-3 (1.025, 1.05) and the 5-yr reduction drops to 29.6%; this is the model's formal statement that crackdown-first backfires. Conclusion: the strategy is effective only within the joint bounds ramp >= 0.5/yr, lag <= 3 yr, treat_rate >= 0.2/yr, and enforcement <= treat_rate; outside these (slow ramp, long lag, weak treatment, or enforcement outrunning care) it underperforms or reverses. This matches the Part 1/2 evidence that the crisis is dynamic (Ohio's 2014-16 surge, VA heroin growth) and that the prescription-to-heroin substitution is the channel a treatment-first, enforcement-bounded strategy is designed to interrupt. Limitations: U_t is a modeled fraction, not a measured count, so the percentages are relative effectiveness, not forecasted case numbers; the backfire coefficient 0.5 is a calibrated placeholder for the substitution effect, not a measured elasticity; the model assumes coverage and treatment act on the same affected population and ignores spatial spillover between counties (the Part 1 spread channel), so a full coupled spatial-strategy model would be a natural extension.
